title: AI is becoming a peace-and-security capability and a source of geopolitical competition faster than multilateral institutions are adapting
source_unit: Security Council Report, Artificial Intelligence, Geopolitics, and the UN Security Council, 15 September 2026
geography: International peace and security, UN Security Council agenda, states, firms, and AI supply chains

observations.period: 2026; AI as conflict-prevention capability and security risk

peace_use.value: AI can support conflict prevention, mediation, peace operations, and sanctions monitoring

risk_use.value: AI can lower barriers to malicious cyber activity and enable misinformation and disinformation at scale

conflict_route.value: the same capabilities can improve early warning and peace work while expanding the speed, scale, and accessibility of hostile operations

boundary.value: the report examines how AI affects peace and security; it does not claim that AI itself determines conflict outcomes

observations.method: Security Council Report policy paper synthesizing AI, international peace and security, UN practice, and policy options.
observations.uncertainty: The paper is a policy analysis rather than an incident dataset, capability benchmark, or causal evaluation of AI in conflict prevention.
observations.subgroup: States, UN peace operations, mediators, sanctions monitors, cyber defenders, armed groups, civilians, and information environments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional safeguards, human review, and targeted use may allow peacebuilding benefits without producing equivalent escalation risks.

denominator.unit: Security Council Report analysis of AI competition

strategic_inputs.value: states and companies compete for semiconductors, computing infrastructure, energy, data, and critical minerals needed to develop and deploy advanced AI

resource_route.value: AI capability is coupled to physical infrastructure, resource access, industrial policy, and supply-chain control

friction.value: competition over AI inputs can become a source of strategic rivalry and geopolitical friction

cross_source_test.value: join AI capability claims to energy demand, data-center buildout, critical minerals, export controls, and public-service or military dependence

observations.method: Security Council Report synthesis of AI capability competition and the material inputs underpinning advanced systems.
observations.uncertainty: The analysis identifies strategic dependencies but does not quantify the probability, timing, or outcome of a specific technology conflict.
observations.subgroup: States, technology firms, chip and mineral suppliers, energy systems, cloud and data-center operators, militaries, and dependent publics.
observations.counterinterpretation: International cooperation, diversified supply chains, open standards, and shared research may reduce rivalry without eliminating competition.

observations.period: 2026; AI, armed conflict, and human control

denominator.unit: Security Council Report analysis of military AI risks

decision_speed.value: AI can compress decision-making timelines in armed conflict

autonomy.value: increasingly autonomous weapons systems raise questions about human oversight, accountability, and compliance with international humanitarian law

human_control.value: advanced systems may diminish human control over consequential decisions and actions

accountability_route.value: the governance problem is not only whether AI works, but where responsibility remains visible when systems act faster and more autonomously

observations.method: Security Council Report policy analysis of AI effects on armed conflict, autonomy, oversight, accountability, and international humanitarian law.
observations.uncertainty: The paper identifies legal and governance questions without resolving how existing law applies to every future system or operational context.
observations.subgroup: Military operators, commanders, civilians, legal authorities, arms-control institutions, technology firms, and affected populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Human-in-the-loop design, strict use constraints, auditability, and accountability mechanisms could preserve meaningful human control.

observations.period: 2023-2026; Security Council engagement and institutional adaptation

denominator.unit: UN Security Council institutional engagement assessment

engagement_status.value: Council engagement with AI has grown since 2023 but remains sporadic, uneven across agenda items, and politically contested

systematic_option.value: the report proposes an Informal Expert Group on Technology, Peace and Security

capacity_functions.value: proposed functions include horizon-scanning, drawing on technical and scientific expertise, and preserving institutional memory across presidencies and membership cycles

legitimacy_route.value: multilateral legitimacy may depend on whether institutions can anticipate AI risks rather than react piecemeal after crises

observations.method: Security Council Report review of Council engagement and practical options for more systematic AI consideration.
observations.uncertainty: The proposed expert group and other options are recommendations, not adopted institutional changes or evidence of future political agreement.
observations.subgroup: Security Council members, UN agencies, technical experts, civil society, states affected by conflict, and publics evaluating multilateral credibility.
observations.counterinterpretation: Existing thematic and country-specific agenda items may provide sufficient entry points if members develop more consistent practice without creating a new body.

related_sources.claim: WEF cybersecurity analysis provides complementary AI, cyber, geopolitics, and resilience context.
OECD space-economy analysis provides complementary infrastructure, supply-chain, and signal-resilience context.

boundary: This record adds an AI-to-peace-and-security route from dual-use capabilities and strategic inputs through cyber, information, military, legal, and multilateral-governance consequences. It is a policy analysis, not a capability test, conflict forecast, incident attribution, legal ruling, or proof that AI causes any particular geopolitical outcome.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Security Council Report publication page and indexed report summary were reviewed for AI peacebuilding uses, cyber and information risks, strategic inputs, armed-conflict autonomy, Council engagement, and proposed institutional options.
